title: How to turn anonymous buyer activity into qualified pipeline
summary: Most B2B buyers research without ever filling out a form. See how Vector routes named, in-market buyers to Sales with context, and revives stalled deals.
body_markdown:
Here’s how pipeline is supposed to happen: a buyer finds you, downloads something, becomes an MQL, and gets routed to Sales.


Here’s how it actually happens: a buyer reads your pricing page, compares you to two competitors, forwards a case study to their boss, and goes quiet. No form, no MQL, no routing. Three weeks later, they sign with someone else.


Your lead routing never saw any of it, because it only starts when someone fills out a form.


## Routing that waits for a hand-raise is routing for the minority


A form fill is a lagging indicator. By the time someone requests a demo, they’ve done most of their research, often with a shortlist already in mind.


The buyers worth catching are the ones still evaluating, and your routing can’t see them. Even when Marketing can see the activity, the follow-up often comes too late. In our[Reality of ABM survey (opens in a new tab)](https://www.vector.co/guides-and-reports/reality-of-abm-report) of 239 demand gen and ABM marketers, only 26.8% said meaningful buyer activity changes an audience, campaign, nurture, or sales action the same day or faster. Another 18.8% said it usually doesn’t get operationalized at all.


One respondent described the cost like this: “By the time signals are compiled and actioned, the buying moment has often passed.”


Vector shows you the named people behind that activity and sends them to HubSpot or Salesforce based on rules you set. Your existing routing takes it from there. The rep gets a person, a role, and what they looked at while[the buyer is still deciding (opens in a new tab)](https://www.vector.co/blog/abm-timing-window) .


## Agree on what earns a handoff


Seeing buyers is half the job. Of the teams we surveyed that collect[website visitor identification data (opens in a new tab)](https://www.vector.co/blog/identify-anonymous-website-visitors) , about 1 in 4 (24.2%) say they rarely act on it. Before you route anything, decide what happens next.


Not every visit deserves a rep’s time. Marketing and Sales should settle three things in one meeting:


-


**Who fits?** The accounts and roles you sell to.


-


**What activity counts?** Repeat visits to pricing, comparison, or integration pages, or a buyer[researching your competitors (opens in a new tab)](https://www.vector.co/blog/b2b-intent-signals-gone-wrong) . A single blog read doesn’t count.


-


**Who owns it?** The account owner if there is one, otherwise a named SDR.


Write it down. If Sales doesn’t agree with the rule, they won’t work the contacts, and you’ll be back in this meeting in a month.


A written rule also takes a job off someone’s plate. About a third of the teams we surveyed (33.1%) still handle the[handoff to outbound (opens in a new tab)](https://www.vector.co/blog/vector-on-vector-how-our-site-visitor-playbook-booked-an-8-meeting-rate-in-two-weeks) manually.


## Start with the deals you already lost


The easiest pipeline to create is pipeline you already had.


Every team has a list of[stalled and closed-lost opportunities (opens in a new tab)](https://www.vector.co/blog/abm-campaign-examples) : deals that died because of timing, budget, or a champion who left. Most of them never get looked at again. Your closed-lost list is full of ghosts, and some of them come back.


If someone from one of those accounts comes back to your pricing page six months later, the rep can pick up where the deal left off instead of starting from scratch.


Vector can watch those accounts and send returning buyers to the original opp owner through your CRM. The rep sees who came back, what they looked at, and whether it’s the same champion or someone new.

## Don’t stop marketing at the handoff


Routing a contact to Sales isn’t the finish line. One person is talking to your rep. Meanwhile, four others are deciding whether to back them.


Vector can build audiences from open and revived opportunities, so Marketing keeps reaching[the rest of the committee (opens in a new tab)](https://www.vector.co/blog/how-to-reach-your-b2b-buying-committee-with-contact-level-ads) while Sales works the conversation. The rep handles the person who came back. Marketing handles everyone else that person has to convince.


The rep handles one. Marketing handles the rest.

## Run it this week


You can set this up in one sitting:


1. 1


**Pull your stalled and closed-lost opps** from the last 12 months.


2. 2


**Set the trigger.** For example, any named contact at one of those accounts visits pricing or comparison pages.


3. 3


**Route it to the original opp owner,** with the contact and pages attached.


4. 4


**Launch an audience** for the rest of that account’s committee.


5. 5


**Review in two weeks.** How many accounts came back? How many reps reached out? How many meetings?


## Measure what the rep did, not what the system did


Routing volume tells you the workflow runs. Rep acceptance, meetings booked, and reopened pipeline tell you it works. Track cycle length too, over a longer window.


Volume shows it runs. Reps show it works.

If reps aren’t acting on the routes, don’t add more. Fix the rule.
